question: A student looks at your name badge and asks, “Have we met before?” What does she want to know?
choices: Whether you arrived before she did.
Whether you’d like to meet after class.
Whether she knows you from another time.
Whether you know anyone else here.
note: She thinks she may recognise you. “Shall we meet later?” would suggest a future meeting.

question: Someone at a party asks, “What sort of music are you into?” What are they asking about?
choices: The music you can play.
The music you’re studying.
The music you can hear now.
The music you enjoy.
note: You can be “into jazz” even if you’ve never played a note. “What do you play?” asks about making music yourself.

question: During a board game, Cem says, “Is it my turn?” What is he checking?
choices: Whether he should play now.
Whether someone wants his seat.
Whether he has won this round.
Whether he chose the right game.
note: Taking turns means doing something one person after another. “Is it my go?” means the same thing here.

picture.alt: A wooden game piece beside a die.

question: “I sold my bike.” “Oh, how come?” What would answer the second speaker’s question?
choices: She took it home on Saturday.
I needed the money for a train pass.
A woman from my street bought it.
It was a blue bike with a basket.
note: “How come?” asks for the reason. “Who bought it?” would invite the answer about the woman.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: Ada says, “I love old films.” Max replies, “So do I.” What has Max told her?
choices: He wants to know why she likes them.
They have seen the same old film.
They both enjoy old films.
He thinks she should try an old film.
note: “So do I” picks up the other person’s statement and says it’s true of you too. It gives them something in common to talk about.

picture.alt: A clapperboard beside a film reel.

question: It’s your first day. A student is sitting alone at lunch with a coat on the chair beside her. All the other seats are taken. What do you say?
choices: Hi, how long are you staying here?
Hi, were you sitting over there before?
Hi, can I move your coat?
Hi, is anyone sitting here?
note: The coat may be saving a place, so “Can I move your coat?” takes the seat before you know. “Is anyone sitting here?” asks first, and lets her say.

picture.alt: A cup of tea on a saucer with loose tea leaves nearby.

question: You ask a new classmate what he did at the weekend. “My uncle took me sailing for the first time,” he says. You’ve always wanted to try it. What do you ask?
choices: What was it like being out on the water?
How often does your uncle visit you?
Did you go to see your uncle again this weekend?
What do you usually do at weekends?
note: “What was it like?” invites him to describe the part you’re curious about. Asking about his usual weekends would move away from this first trip.

question: You’re introducing a new classmate. You can read her name on her badge, but music covered her voice when she said it. You’re unsure how to pronounce it. What do you say?
choices: Sorry, would you mind spelling your name for me?
Sorry, could you say your name again?
Sorry, shall we do the introductions after the music stops?
Sorry, have you met my friend before?
note: Hearing the name again helps you pronounce it in the introduction. Asking her to spell it would help if you needed to write it down. Here you can already read it on her badge.

question: Your partner says, “I buy old records at the Sunday market.” You buy yours there too. You’d like to compare the records you’ve found. What do you say?
choices: I’ve heard of it. Do they sell anything else?
I like markets. How do you get there?
I go there too! What’s your best find so far?
I go there too! What time does it close?
note: “Your best find” asks about a record worth talking about. Asking when the market closes would help you plan a visit.

question: At lunch, a new classmate says, “I still haven’t worked out how to get to the other side of the city.” You take the ferry there every day. What do you say?
choices: Which side did you like better when you went?
That sounds interesting. Why did you move here?
How long have you been taking the ferry?
Where do you need to go? The ferry might work.
note: The destination matters before you can suggest a route. “Why did you move here?” could start another conversation, but your classmate still needs a way across.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: “So I opened the book and a photo fell out.” You both start talking at once. You want to hear whose photo it was. What do you say?
choices: Sorry, go on. What happened next?
Sorry, let me tell mine first.
Sorry, shall we leave it there?
Sorry, where did you buy the book?
note: “Go on” gives the speaker the floor again. “Shall we leave it there?” would bring the story to an end just as it gets interesting.

picture.alt: An open storybook with a little castle rising from its pages.

question: A new student tells you she spends every Sunday playing tennis. You’ve never played, but you wonder why she loves it. What do you say?
choices: So do I. What time do you normally finish?
I’ve never tried it. What do you like about it?
Same here. Where do you usually play?
I’ve never tried it. Is the court near here?
note: You can show interest without claiming to share the hobby. The question about the court would be useful if you wanted directions.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: You ask to see your partner’s family photos. “I’d rather keep those private,” he says. Earlier he mentioned taking photos of buildings. What do you say?
choices: Fair enough. Why do you keep those pictures private?
No problem. Could you send me the photos later?
Of course. Have you taken any good city photos lately?
I see. Could I just look at one family photo?
note: City photos give him a subject he’s happy to share. Asking why all his family photos are private keeps him on the subject he tried to leave.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: Leyla and Tom both paint. You know them, but they’ve never met. They’re standing together at an art show. What do you say?
choices: Tom, Leyla paints too. Have you seen this picture?
Leyla, Tom paints too. Shall we all go for coffee?
Tom, let me show you what Leyla’s been painting.
Tom, this is Leyla. She paints too.
note: “This is Leyla” introduces them, and painting gives them a first topic. Asking whether Tom has seen a picture gives him a topic but still leaves Leyla without an introduction.

question: You’ve enjoyed talking to a new neighbour on the platform. Your train arrives. Hers leaves from the other side. What do you say?
choices: That’s my train. Nice talking to you!
Shall we catch this one together?
I’ll see you when we get off, then.
I’d love to hear the rest. Shall we keep talking?
note: “Nice talking to you” ends a first chat warmly. “Shall we catch this one together?” would suit two people travelling the same way.

picture.alt: Steps and railings at an underground railway entrance.
